baselines.name: current text
baselines.text:
Most people hear "model" and think of a chat model. This is a different kind. It reads your text and your labels together, as one input, and gives each label a score for how well it fits. It never writes text. It cannot answer with a label you did not give it.

It works like a multiple-choice question. Your text is the question and your labels are the choices. With one label, the model marks one choice. With several labels, it marks every choice that applies, or none. Where the comparison stops: a person thinks the question through, while the model scores each choice from patterns it learned in training and does not check whether anything is true.

This kind of model is called a classifier. You write the list of labels, and it decides which of them fit:

gliner-runner classify --labels billing,support,shipping "I was charged twice for my last order."
billing (confidence 0.889)

The labels are billing, support, and shipping. The answer is billing.

baselines.name: landing lead
baselines.text: Tossing the junk mail before you reach the front door. You make calls like this all day without thinking. GLiNER Runner makes them about text: give it a message and a few labels, and it tells you which one fits, such as billing or shipping, urgent or can wait, positive or negative.

baselines.name: user's words, lightly cut
baselines.text: This is a thinking-fast model. It does something people do in their heads all the time. Nobody wakes up wanting to sort things into labels. But you do it all day.

baselines.text: You send a text and a few labels. You get back the label that fits, and a score for each one. Before you trust it with a job, or build on it, know what those scores mean, what the program cannot do, how much text it can read, and how fast it is.
